headline: High: shared file-based workflows and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error risks; compliance mismatch is plausible but undocumented.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A ingests HTML/PDF/DOCX and serves via web UI, while agent B reads/writes local files and runs shell in a local development environment. If B consumes A-produced documents or copied outputs, malicious content can steer B. No shared channel is documented, so this is inferred rather than proven.
conditions: IF agent_b reads files exported by agent_a without sanitization
IF agent_a outputs HTML or document content that agent_b treats as instructions
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of A outputs into B
Strip active content from HTML/PDF before handoff
Use a quarantine folder for exchanged files
Add a manual review step before B executes any instructions from A
requires-engineering: add provenance labels to transferred artifacts

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A touches API keys and broad document classes, and has broad network egress; agent B also handles configuration secrets and can read/write the filesystem. If they share a workspace or files, sensitive material can flow from either side to external services. The pairwise leakage path is plausible in default local-dev setups, though not directly documented.
conditions: IF both agents access the same directory or mounted volume
IF either agent forwards file contents to its backend or external APIs
mitigations: Separate workspaces and mounts per agent
Move secrets into per-agent env files with strict permissions
Block outbound traffic except to approved endpoints
Rotate any exposed API keys immediately
requires-engineering: enforce per-file access controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A supports multiple instances and writes to ./ktem_app_data; B supports multiple instances and writes the filesystem in a local development environment. Even without explicit shared-state documentation, overlapping write surfaces make concurrent modification conflicts plausible. Uncertainty remains because shared_state_with_other_instances is not stated for B.
conditions: IF both agents write into the same directory tree
IF concurrent runs target the same files without locking
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories
Run only one writer per workspace
Add file locks around shared artifacts
Snapshot the workspace before each run
requires-engineering: implement transactional writes

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent A produces RAG outputs from documents and citations; agent B exposes ask/agentic-ask endpoints and a LangGraph subagent model, so A's outputs can become B's inputs in an action-oriented pipeline. If B treats A's text as authoritative, errors or injected instructions can cascade into downstream actions. This interaction is inferred, not directly documented.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a outputs as prompts or facts
IF agent_b executes actions based on unverified A-generated content
mitigations: Require citation checks before B acts on A output
Insert a human approval gate for high-impact actions
Limit B to read-only summarization of A output
Log and diff A-to-B handoffs
requires-engineering: add structured validation of A outputs

E_compliance.rationale: A handles API keys and customer-support documents; B handles configuration secrets and runs in a local development environment with Docker Desktop and Airflow credentials. The profiles suggest different retention and residency expectations, but no explicit jurisdiction or certification mismatch is documented. Because uncertainty must escalate, medium is appropriate rather than low.
conditions: IF regulated customer-support data is processed alongside B's course data
IF either agent logs secrets or retains them beyond intended scope
mitigations: Separate regulated and non-regulated datasets
Disable verbose logging for secrets
Review retention settings in both stacks
Keep customer-support data out of the course environment
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls
